steps.title: Brownian motion
steps.body: The random, zigzag motion of particles in a fluid (liquid or gas), caused by collisions with much smaller, fast-moving particles. This provides evidence for the particle model of matter.

steps.title: Gas pressure
steps.body: The force exerted by gas particles per unit area on the walls of a container, caused by particles colliding with the walls.

steps.title: Absolute zero
steps.body: The lowest possible temperature (−273°C or 0 K), at which particles have zero kinetic energy and stop moving.

steps.title: Kelvin scale
steps.body: A temperature scale that starts at absolute zero. An increase of 1 K is the same as an increase of 1°C.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Gas particles are in constant random motion. When they collide with the walls of their container, they exert a force on the wall. The pressure is this force per unit area. p = F / A p = pressure (Pa), F = force (N), A = area (m²) How gas pressure arises: Gas particles collide with the walls of the container. Each collision exerts a tiny force. Billions of collisions per second add up to produce the overall gas pressure. The pressure depends on how hard and how often the particles hit the walls.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Foundation Describe what causes gas pressure in a sealed container. | Foundation Explain how Brownian motion provides evidence for the particle model. | Higher A gas at 150 kPa has a volume of 4.0 m³. The volume is reduced to 1.5 m³ at constant temperature. Calculate the new pressure.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Gas particles are in constant random motion. They collide with the walls of the container, exerting a force on them. The total force per unit area of the wall is the gas pressure. | Brownian motion shows larger particles (e.g. smoke) moving in random zigzag paths. This is caused by collisions with smaller, invisible air or water particles. This random, uneven bombardment can only | p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ → 150 × 4.0 = p₂ × 1.5 → 600 = 1.5 p₂ → p₂ = 400 kPa

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When explaining gas pressure, always mention particles colliding with walls — not just "particles moving" Boyle's Law only works at constant temperature and for a fixed mass of gas — check these conditions before using p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ Always convert temperatures to Kelvin before using proportional relationships — pressure is proportional to Kelvin temperature, not Celsius temperature In Brownian motion questions, make clear the distinction between the small, invisible particles (air/water) and the larger, visible particles (smoke/pollen) Remember: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa. Make sure all pressures are in the same units before calculating When asked to explain pressure changes, always link back to frequency of collisions and/or force of collisions
